input: When it comes to the analysis of a powder blend, it is important to note that the sampling step is arguably the most crucial stage of the whole procedure, because no amount of sophisticated laboratory analysis can compensate for a sample that does not faithfully represent the material from which it was drawn. A powder blend, despite appearances, is rarely the perfectly uniform mixture that one might assume: during handling, transport, and storage, the finer particles gradually percolate downwards through the gaps between the larger particles, while the coarser particles tend to migrate outwards towards the walls and upwards towards the surface, thereby creating composition differences from place to place within the container. In light of this, good practice is to collect a series of small portions, referred to as increments, from a variety of different locations, for instance near the top, around the middle, and near the bottom of the container, or, alternatively, at intervals across the stream as the blender discharges its contents. These increments are then combined together and mixed thoroughly in order to form a single composite sample, which is subsequently reduced down to the size needed for the assay by a technique, such as riffling, that does not separate the particles according to their size. By contrast, a single grab sample, scooped hastily from one convenient spot, can be deeply misleading, since it captures only the local composition at that one place and moment: material taken from the surface will over-represent the coarse fraction, material taken from near the bottom will over-represent the fines, and the resulting figure gives no indication whatsoever that anything is amiss, presenting a varying blend as though it were perfectly uniform. Ultimately, then, it is by sampling from several positions, combining the increments, and reducing the composite with care that the analyst obtains a portion that genuinely reflects the batch as a whole, ensuring that the assay result can be relied upon.
target:
A powder blend assay is trusted only as far as the sample represents the batch. Sampling of a powder blend therefore builds one sample from increments taken at several positions, so that the assay portion carries the composition of the blend as a whole.

A blend is not uniform throughout its container. Fine particles percolate downward through the voids between coarser particles during handling and storage, and coarse particles migrate toward the surface and the walls, so the composition at any one position differs from the composition elsewhere.

Increments are taken near the top, at mid-depth, and near the bottom of the container, or at intervals across the stream while the blender discharges. Each increment is small compared with the batch, and the increments are spread so that the combined sample covers every region of the container. The increments are combined and mixed, and the combined sample is reduced to the assay portion by a method that does not sort the particles, such as riffling.

A single grab sample misleads because it reports the composition at one position and one moment. A scoop from the surface overstates the coarse fraction; a scoop from the bottom overstates the fines. The result carries no sign of its own bias, and a blend that varies across the container is reported as uniform. Where the blend is sampled decides what the assay can show, and the analysis that follows cannot correct a biased portion. Sampling at several positions, combining the increments, and reducing the combined sample without segregation gives an assay portion from which the batch can be judged.
